source.title: Constructed Ownership — from Checkpoint 10 and Comparative Dossier
source.author: Codex

claims.claim_text: First-personality must be decomposed into at least five distinct senses: P_S (sensorimotor perspectivity — information organized from here), P_G (phenomenal givenness — the state is manifest), P_A (affective concern — the state matters relative to this organism), P_O (ownership — the state is intrinsically mine), P_I (autobiographical identification — the state is attributed to this represented person). The inferential order is NOT P_S = P_G = P_A = P_O = P_I. Rather: P_S ⇏ P_G ⇏ P_A ⇏ P_O ⇏ P_I. A system can be functionally centred without being conscious (P_S without P_G). A conscious state may be manifest without representing an ego (P_G without P_O). A valenced state may contribute to constructing ownership rather than presupposing an owner (P_A contributes to P_O, not the reverse). This decomposition pressures any theory that moves too quickly from 'experience has a perspective' to 'experience has an owner.'
claims.hetu: first-personality admits of at least five distinct senses
claims.sadhya: ownership is not a simple primitive
claims.vyapti_statement: If first-personality decomposes into separable aspects, then theories treating it as a single primitive (either constitutive or constructed) must specify which aspect they address.

falsifier.condition: Show a single phenomenal state that inseparably possesses all five aspects of first-personality in a way that precludes any functional decomposition.

claims.reasoning: This decomposition is one of Checkpoint 10's key results. It blocks the quick inference from 'reflexivity' to 'subject.'

source_span.quote: selected sign → feeling → valuation → appropriation → self-involving proliferation

claims.claim_text: Ñāṇananda's analysis permits a construction model: nimitta (selected sign) → vedanā (feeling) → valuation → appropriation → self-involving proliferation (papañca). Modern interoceptive predictive accounts converge: predictions about the body's internal state generate affect, which grounds mineness. The resulting loop is: organismic concern → self-relative valuation → operative centre → further self-relative valuation. This explains affective and functional ownership better than it explains manifestness. It does not establish why the valuation loop is experienced. Thus: ownership may be constructed within manifestation, while manifestation itself remains unexplained.
claims.hetu: valuation and appropriation can construct ownership
claims.sadhya: but do not explain why the construction is manifest
claims.vyapti_statement: If ownership can be constructed through valuation and appropriation, then manifestness must be explained separately from ownership.

falsifier.condition: Show that a complete account of ownership (including its manifest character) can be derived from valuation and appropriation alone, without a primitive manifestness.

claims.reasoning: This is the constructed ownership frontier. Enactivist and Buddhist models explain the structure of ownership ('mine-ness') but not why the construction is felt rather than merely computed.

source_span.quote: Does something matter because it is experienced by a subject, or does recurrent mattering stabilize the local subject?

claims.claim_text: The relation between mattering (valuation, concern) and subjecthood is bidirectional. Question: does something matter because it is experienced by a pre-existing subject, or does recurrent mattering stabilize the local subject as a dynamical structure? If mattering stabilizes the subject, then the subject is not the precondition of experience but an emergent organization within it. This is the Ñāṇananda-enactivist branch and it directly bears on perspectival partition: if subjects are stabilized by recurrent patterns of concern, then partition (exclusion) may be grounded in divergent patterns of what matters — different organisms care about different things, and this difference in concern partially explains why phenomenal domains are exclusive.
claims.hetu: different organisms care about different things
claims.sadhya: this difference in concern may partially explain phenomenal exclusion
claims.vyapti_statement: If subjects are stabilized by patterns of concern, and different organisms have different patterns of concern, then divergent concern partially explains why phenomenal domains are exclusive.

falsifier.condition: Show two organisms with identical patterns of concern that nevertheless have exclusive phenomenal domains, proving that divergent concern is insufficient to explain partition.

claims.reasoning: This is a speculative but important constraint on Λ. If mattering-stabilizes-subject is true, then Λ must include a dimension of concern/valuation.
